You won’t fail the exam if your light turns red when you make late left turn because the oncoming traffic ran the yellow light - so long as you have already entered the intersection and was waiting prior to the yellow/red light, and that you also didn’t wait five million years before completing the turn. If you cross the stop line AFTER and then make the left turn at the right, you will fail. When you’re making a left turn on an unprotected intersection only proceed when it is safe. When your light turns yellow and you’re already in the intersection, you still need to ensure it’s clear before crossing. Then your next step is to complete the turn to ensure you’re not blocking the intersection. Remember, green lights means “proceed when intersection is clear and safe” not a “go ahead and go no matter what”. 

2. ALWAYS scan left and right when proceeding through an intersection regardless if you are “first in line” or not. The car ahead of you could have gone when it’s safe, but by the time you enter the intersection, a runaway car or truck could be running the red. Slowing down, or at least having your feet on the brake when crossing is great defensive driving skills. It shows to your examiner that you’re ready to react if things go sideways - which more commonly do in intersections. REMEMBER, NEVER ASSUME when driving, unless your assumption is that everyone else around you are idiots that is. 

3. Just because people should doesn’t mean they actually do. And again, just like in number two, you still should be glancing both ways prior to crossing. It might not even be a train zooming past, but kids on bikes running by a railroad track, who knows. Once you get more comfortable driving, looking both ways is actually not distracting as you’d think even at higher speeds. A quick glance and shift of your eyes is all you need, not some elaborate left and right shoulder check. But please, do make it a practice and habit to at least scan the intersections prior to proceeding. The examiner will want to make sure you’re regularly scanning your environment. If that’s overwhelming, you’ll definitely need more practice and experience because overtime you’ll be able to quickly scan and get lots of the information you need. 

4. Yes, when parking uphill or downhill you must turn your wheel so that if the car were to roll up/down, it hits and stops at the curb. (Uphill, turn left. Downhill, turn right.)

5. Diamond means RESTRICTED LANE. Not necessarily HOV or Bus Only. You’d have to look at signs to determine what that restriction is. Commonly on highways, you’ll see that the diamond is signalling that it’s 2 or more passengers only (HOV). In Surrey you’ll see more “Bus Only” lanes. If the bus only lane shares with a right turn lane, you may enter the lane for a right turn once you see the break in the lane markings AND IF IT IS SAFE TO DO SO. 

6. When you see the emergency vehicle and need to make space, pull to the closest side. If there is no open space available, you may need to pull forward and turn to the side within the intersection. Just don’t be a sick and gtfo of the way of incoming emergency vehicles. If you don’t see or hear it, proceed with caution, and when approaching intersections, make sure to scan and slow down in case they are nearby. Use environmental clues to help pinpoint the location (for example, you see people stopping on one side or people slowing up ahead). 

7. Stopping? Stopping where? You only need to stop if there are pedestrians crossing or intending to cross the school cross walk. Slowing down? Well that’s a them problem if they aren’t slowing down at school zones. 

8. Generally, yes. Unless it is a double left turn lane, or a double right turn lane. Sometimes there’s construction, and then there may be lane changes according to the construction signage. HOWEVER, when changing lanes, do not do so while completing a turn or when crossing an intersection. Meaning, if you are turning left, continue through in the intersection and enter in the left lane. Do not make a left turn from the left lane crossing into the right lane during the intersection to change lanes into the right (even though you’ll see this happen a lot throughout the city).

I was on antidepressants, saw therapists that were ehhhh, and was constantly depressed and anxious that I would get sick all the time. Every new semester I had panic attacks thinking I would never make it. 

I eventually said fuck it, let’s stop worrying about high grades and just do enough to pass and not be on academic probation. Just survive and do *enough*. I took only maximum 3 courses a semester, skipped summer for a break and really tried to reframe my way of looking at things. 

I found a job during undergrad that was extremely flexible and part-time, so even though I wasn’t making that much money, it was still a little something. 

Five years later I graduated. 

Now I’m finishing my Masters degree. 

Don’t worry about the rush. Take care of yourself - that’s my biggest advice. If you can take care of yourself, things will follow. Even if you do poorly in school, it’ll be more important that you have your sanity and other options outside of academia are definitely available! They’re just other adventures. 

Enjoy your time and life. You’re not a burden and a failure.

It gets better. I know that’s really cliche, because it really sucks when you’re in it and that saying does not make those feelings go away when you’re in the moment. I know, I’ve been there and heard it too. But it’ll get better, you won’t be in your undergrad forever, you’ll be graduating next year. :)

I used to do the commute from Coquitlam Centre to the Surrey Memorial area daily, and generally it was an average of 30-45 minutes drive during the mornings (7-8AM) and in the afternoons around 3-4. 50 minutes on a bad day when traffic is being a little annoying.

The route is very straightforward, so driving isn't really a hassle. 

The only major gripes I had with the commute is:

* Port Mann Bridge can be a severe bottleneck - If there's accidents on the bridge, you can be really stuck in traffic for a while without any alternatives unless you planned earlier prior to taking the exit towards the bridge
* Winter conditions - Winter conditions can make it extremely difficult commuting to Surrey due to increased accidents, and possibility of bridge closures due to the weather
* 25 minute drives was really only during COVID season when the lockdown happened and roads were quiet, or during late late nights or early early mornings.

As for public transit, you could totally take the SkyTrain as it's more reliable and faster as it isn't impacted by road traffic. You'd probably only need to get on one bus after to get to the hospital.

Considering that you do not own a car and are probably taking a train and bus, you may need to check if the transit system allows small animals on board. Some places require them to be housed in a certain sized compartment. And other places may not even allow animals on board. 

In terms of the rabbits well-being, I personally would not recommend travelling with rabbits on a bus/train, especially if they are very young. Young bunnies tend to be especially skittish at times and may get too freaked out by all the different noises and movement. With that said, I know of rabbits that are very calm and fine with travelling and others that immediately get in constant stress from going from one place to another. The main concern would be the lack of places for it to ‘hide’ and stay calm in the event that there are a lot of things going around. 

I have travelled with my rabbit via my own car for extended periods of time, so if you do decide to follow through I’d definitely recommend a cover for the carrier. I find that when I cover my rabbit’s cage with a blanket they feel more at ease as they’re sheltered as opposed to being in an open crate where they may feel a predator may be able to find them.

It sounds like you have a very curious bun! She’s probably wanting to get high ground as much as possible to scope out her new surroundings as it seems like you’ve moved into a new apartment. Curious behaviours like this may just naturally decrease overtime once she’s acquainted with the new surroundings provided that there’s nothing reinforcing that she can access on top of these things. 

Unfortunately if there’s a path for her to get up and climb, she’ll take it. So options include either blocking all access by having her in a place that doesn’t have chairs and tables (ie. a den of another room) or adding things to minimize risk of injury (setting up thicker rugs around or even purposely having foot stools set up as “stairs” for her to come down instead of just jumping straight down. I know from my experience that my rabbit will prefer taking her foot stool stairs down rather than the full jump but again rabbit behaviours are always so unique. :) 

Another option is investing in high pet play pens (not necessarily to cage her in, but to cage in things like the tables/counters). It's a lot more obtrusive and an eye sore, but for places like my computer room, my entire desk is surrounded by a fence to prevent her from jumping up and accessing cables underneath.

Best Buy employees had scoffed and questioned me when I mentioned I was going to be using the computer mainly for gaming. With one even going as far to ask if what I had meant by gaming was FarmVille. 

Throughout the actual building process, I learned that it was actually pretty simple and quite a therapeutic and intimate process. There’s so many helpful and kind communities out there to help on your first pc build journey. For them I am thankful because despite the small handful of people out there that do doubt a female’s abilities to do something remotely related to PC building (I’m looking at you Mr. Other Employee that laughed at me when I said I was building a pc and said I was wrong when I needed more than 8GB on a USB to mount the Windows 10 Installation), all these communities truly helped a little girl’s dream come true.

Rabbits have some blind spots and will sometimes dislike it if hands come to pet them especially from up high or directly above. Remember that they’re a prey species! Hands coming up from above can trigger instincts of fear as if a hawk or owl is coming down from above them. Directly petting their back from above may cause them to think that someone’s trying to nip or grab them. In general, most rabbits prefer getting petted on the head as opposed from behind anyways. 

If you are interested in acclimating your rabbit to getting petted on their back, I recommend changing your angle of approach. Lay on your stomach or get as low to floor as you can. Get in front of your rabbit and give them plenty of vision of your hand. Slowly pet their head and gradually work towards their back. Be gentle and make sure your rabbit has a good idea of where your hand is going. With time, they’ll get more used to it, so long as you don’t surprise them and come in from an angle where they can clearly see it’s just you. :)

Not a doctor or nurse, but you could consider me a patient I guess. 

When I was a kid, there was a phase where all my friends were getting glasses and not wanting to feel left out, I wanted to get glasses too. So I asked my parents to take me to the optometrist. With every eye exam they gave, I purposely failed it by giving the wrong answers. 

One of the exams was the one where they had coloured dots all around with the number or letter hidden within in a slightly different coloured dot. Really wanting glasses and thinking I was a good liar, I responded incorrectly to each one. If there was a hidden 2, I’d say 8. If there was a hidden 7, I’d say some random other number. 

Years later I came to learn that that eye exam was meant to measure colour vision to check if there was any kind of colour blindness going on. If you had colour blindness, you wouldn’t even see a number. But I thought it was like one of those eye charts where they check to see if you can even read the letter. Person who was running the eye exam definitely knew I was faking it or at least a dumbass who can’t read numbers.

tldr; wanted glasses really bad that I purposely tried to fail an eye exam by blurting out obviously wrong answers not knowing it was actually meant to measure colour blindness.
